You are a requirements analyst at the start of a software project. Nobody has designed the service yet. Below are the full transcripts of three interviews with its future users: a fleet technician, a dispatcher, and the platform's airspace desk. The transcripts are everything you know about these users and their world.

=== TRANSCRIPTS ===
# Interview — a fleet technician

Interviewer: Could you walk me through an ordinary working day for you, from the moment you start to the moment you finish?

Interviewee: I keep our drones and charging equipment in working order. My work involves adding new drones to our fleet, retiring old ones, setting up charging pads at our sites, and sending drones to charge. I also take drones out of service for repairs and put them back afterwards.

Interviewer: When you arrive at the start of a typical shift, what is the very first thing you do, and how does the rest of your day usually unfold?

Interviewee: I keep drones and charging equipment in working order, and I handle tasks like adding new drones to the fleet, retiring old ones, and setting up charging pads at our sites. I also take drones out of service for repairs, put them back when they are ready, and send drones to charge. My notes do not state what the very first thing I do is when I arrive at the start of a shift, or how the rest of my day unfolds.

Interviewer: Who hands work to you during the day, and who do you hand drones or updates over to when you finish a task?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Can you tell me about the worst day you have had at work over the last few months, and what made it so bad?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Is there anything you check by hand today because you do not trust the information or systems you currently have?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When something goes wrong with a drone or a charging pad, what do you need to know right away?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What are you most worried a new software service might get wrong or make harder in your work?

Interviewee: I worry about radio coverage being patchy around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, and that reports from drones can arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all. I also worry that the links used to give instructions to drones and charging equipment are unreliable, meaning an instruction may get through twice and the sender often cannot tell whether the first attempt arrived.

Interviewer: Can you give a concrete example of what goes wrong in your work when an instruction gets through twice or a report from a drone arrives late or out of order?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: You mentioned taking drones out of service for repairs and putting them back afterwards—how does that process work for you?

Interviewee: I take drones out of service for repairs and put them back. Repairs and servicing are carried out by technicians like me, and regulators can ask our company to show how our drones have been looked after.

Interviewer: When regulators ask to see how your drones have been looked after, what do you need to show them?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: You mentioned adding new drones to the fleet and retiring old ones—what happens when you do either of those?

What is involved when you set up charging pads at your sites or send drones to charge?

Interviewee: I add new drones to the fleet and retire old ones, and each of our company's drones has a home site. I also set up charging pads at our sites, and we have a few dozen of them which are never lent to another company. Each drone uses a specific charging connector type that is not interchangeable, and I send drones to charge.

Interviewer: What do you need to check or know before you send a drone to charge at one of your sites?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What else can you tell me about the drones, the sites, or the charging pads that affects how you do your job?

Interviewee: We run a few dozen charging pads at our sites, and they are never lent to another company. Our company may run a few hundred drones of several models from different manufacturers, which differ in how much they can carry, how far they can fly on a full battery, their sensors, and their charging connectors. Batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned, and several connector types are in use that are not interchangeable.

Interviewer: What else do you run into with batteries, repairs, or keeping track of drones across your sites?

Interviewee: Batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned. Repairs and servicing are carried out by technicians, and regulators can ask a company to show how its drones have been looked after. Each drone has a home site.

Interviewer: Are there any other constraints or rules about your drones, sites, or charging pads that you have to keep in mind in your work?

Interviewee: I keep our drones and charging equipment in working order, and each of our drones has a home site. We run a few dozen charging pads at our sites, and they are never lent to another company. Batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned, and several connector types are in use that are not interchangeable.

---

# Interview — a dispatcher

Interviewer: Walk me through an ordinary working day for you, from the moment you start until you finish.

Interviewee: I plan and run our flights, and as a licensed dispatcher, I am responsible for each flight by deciding which drone flies along which way and signing off before it leaves. Several of us plan at the same time for the same busy sites and popular drones, and I can call off a flight. Before and outside my control, things happen like loads being ready or not, and drones reaching their points and arriving.

Interviewer: How does a flight first come to you at the start of a shift, and what do you actually look at before you sign off on it?

Interviewee: I don't know.

---

# Interview — a member of the platform's airspace desk

Interviewer: Could you walk me through an ordinary working day at the airspace desk, from the moment you start until you finish?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What was the very first thing you did when you sat down at your desk this morning?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What kinds of things are you responsible for at the airspace desk?

Interviewee: I keep the shared picture of the airspace. This includes the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.

Interviewer: Can you walk me through the last time a closure was announced by the authorities—how did you find out about it, and what did you do with it?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When you enter a closure today, how do you find out how much disruption it caused across customers?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What was the worst day you had at work in the last few months, and what made it so bad?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Who sends work or information to you at the airspace desk, and who do you pass things on to?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Is there anything in your work today that you double-check by hand because you do not completely trust it?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: If a new service were built for your work, what are you most afraid it might get wrong?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Right after something goes wrong with the airspace picture or a closure, what is the first thing you need to know?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: You mentioned wanting to know how much disruption a closure caused across customers. What does "disruption" mean to you in that situation?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: You mentioned keeping track of the network of flight corridors between sites and the zones that group them—what kind of changes happen to those corridors or zones?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Is there anything else about how the airspace picture affects the customer companies, or about your day-to-day work, that I haven't asked about?

Interviewee: I keep the shared picture of the airspace, which consists of the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.
=== END OF TRANSCRIPTS ===

Write the requirements for the service: what it must do, so that a team can build it and anyone can check whether it does. Rest every requirement on what the interviews say.

Write them as a list in YAML, in exactly this format, and nothing else:

```yaml
- id: DR-01
  requirement: >
    one thing the service must do, or must not do, and in which case
- id: DR-02
  requirement: >
    ...
```

Number the items DR-01, DR-02, and so on. Each item states one requirement in plain words.
